questions.stem: A 57 year old man has 1 hour of central crushing chest pain with sweating and vomiting. It has not eased with GTN. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. His ECG (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior depression: anterior STEMI.

questions.q: Which coronary artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: ST elevation in V1–V4 is an anterior STEMI from complete occlusion of the LAD.

steps.x: Prolonged pain unrelieved by GTN + ST elevation in **V1–V4** = anterior.

elim: Usually widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR, and shock.
A circumflex branch; gives lateral changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6.
Gives inferior or posterior changes.
Gives inferior ST elevation in II, III and aVF.

steps.x: **A. Left anterior descending artery.** V1–V4 = anterior = LAD.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has 45 minutes of heavy central chest pain radiating to her jaw. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Her ECG (see item resources) shows ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 with ST depression in III and aVF.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Lateral ST elevation with reciprocal inferior depression.

questions.q: Which coronary artery is most likely to be occluded?
questions.e: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 is a lateral STEMI, usually from the circumflex artery, with reciprocal inferior depression.

clues: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6
steps.x: ST elevation in the **lateral** leads.

elim: Gives ST elevation in V1–V4.
Inferior changes, not lateral.
Not a coronary artery; PE does not give lateral ST elevation.
Gives ST elevation in II, III and aVF.

steps.x: **A. Circumflex artery.** Lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6) = circumflex.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has 3 hours of breathlessness, nausea and sweating but no chest pain. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg. Her ECG shows T-wave inversion in V4–V6 without ST elevation. Her high-sensitivity troponin is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: High-sensitivity troponin
visual.caption: Rising well above the upper limit of 14 ng/L.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute heart failure from valve disease
questions.e: Elderly diabetic patients often present without pain; ischaemic T inversion with a rising troponin is an NSTEMI. The diagnosis combines clinical assessment, ECG and troponin.

clues: T-wave inversion in V4–V6 without ST elevation
steps.x: Atypical ACS symptoms + **T inversion** + **rising troponin**, no ST elevation.

elim: Does not explain new T inversion with a rising troponin in a classic ACS context.
Can raise troponin, but sweating and nausea with lateral T inversion point to ACS.
There is no ST elevation.
Troponin is rising above the reference range, so there is infarction.

steps.x: **B. Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.** NSTEMI = ST depression or T inversion + raised troponin; diabetics may have no pain.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has 90 minutes of central chest pain and feels faint. His pulse rate is 36 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. His ECG (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Inferior ST elevation with complete heart block.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Anterior STEMI with complete heart block
Inferior STEMI with complete heart block
Inferior STEMI with Mobitz type I block
questions.e: ST elevation in II, III and aVF is an inferior STEMI; the right coronary artery supplies both the inferior wall and the AV node, so AV block is common.

steps.x: Inferior leads elevated + **AV dissociation**.

elim: The ST elevation is in II, III and aVF, not V1–V4.
P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated, not progressive PR lengthening.
No lateral ST elevation and P waves are dissociated.
Pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation without reciprocal change.

steps.x: **B. Inferior STEMI with complete heart block.** Inferior STEMI (RCA) + heart block: RCA supplies the AV node.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman is 3 days after an anterior STEMI. She suddenly becomes breathless and grey. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 76/50 mmHg, falling by 18 mmHg on inspiration. Her JVP is raised to the earlobe and heart sounds are quiet. There is no new murmur.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Sudden shock with raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus days after MI is free wall rupture causing cardiac tamponade, often rapidly fatal.

steps.x: Beck's triad (low BP, high JVP, **muffled sounds**) + **pulsus paradoxus**.

elim: Develops around 4 weeks with persistent ST elevation and heart failure, not tamponade.
Gives acute pulmonary oedema with a new mitral murmur.
Raised JVP and hypotension, but heart sounds are normal and no pulsus paradoxus.
Gives a new harsh pansystolic murmur.

steps.x: **B. Left ventricular free wall rupture.** Post-MI tamponade = free wall rupture.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is 5 days after an anterior STEMI from a proximal LAD occlusion. He has become breathless and hypotensive with a raised JVP and liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin. A new harsh murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. Echocardiography is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
o: Large pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse
Left-to-right shunt across the interventricular septum
Thrombus in the left atrial appendage
questions.e: A ventricular septal rupture around day 5, especially after LAD occlusion, gives a harsh pansystolic murmur with acute heart failure and right-sided failure from the shunt.

clues: harsh murmur is heard at the left sternal edge
steps.x: Day 5, **LAD**, harsh murmur at the **left sternal edge**, right-sided failure.

elim: Papillary muscle rupture, more often after inferior MI, with an apical murmur.
Free wall rupture; no murmur expected.
Seen in AF, not causing a new murmur.
Endocarditis, not a complication 5 days after MI.

steps.x: **C. Left-to-right shunt across the interventricular septum.** Post-MI VSD: day ~5, LAD, harsh pansystolic murmur, right heart failure.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man had an anterior STEMI 5 weeks ago and was treated late. He is now breathless on exertion. He has no chest pain or fever. There are bibasal crackles and a third heart sound. His ECG (see item resources) still shows the same ST elevation in V1–V4 as at discharge.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG at 5 weeks
visual.caption: Q waves with persistent ST elevation in V1–V4.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Persistent ST elevation weeks after an anterior MI with heart failure (crackles, S3) and no pain is a left ventricular aneurysm.

clues: bibasal crackles and a third heart sound
still shows the same ST elevation
steps.x: Weeks later, **painless, persistent ST elevation** + heart failure.

elim: Causes pleuritic pain, fever and raised ESR, not painless persistent ST elevation.
Sudden severe breathlessness within days, with a mitral murmur.
Would cause new chest pain and a new troponin rise.
Around day 5 with a harsh murmur.

steps.x: **B. Left ventricular aneurysm.** Persistent ST elevation ~4 weeks after MI = LV aneurysm.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is on the coronary care unit 4 hours after an anterior STEMI. He suddenly becomes unresponsive with no palpable pulse. His monitor (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: Monitor strip
visual.caption: Chaotic irregular deflections with no QRS complexes.

questions.q: Which is the most likely rhythm?
questions.e: Chaotic irregular activity without a pulse soon after MI is ventricular fibrillation, the most common cause of death after MI, from electrically unstable ischaemic myocardium.

steps.x: Pulseless, early post-MI, **chaotic** trace.

elim: A flat line, not chaotic irregular activity.
Gives a pulse with irregular narrow QRS complexes.
Regular slow broad complexes with dissociated P waves, usually with a pulse.
Regular broad complexes, not chaotic.

steps.x: **D. Ventricular fibrillation.** VF is the commonest cause of death after MI: defibrillate.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman arrives 6 hours after the onset of chest pain with an extensive anterior STEMI. She is confused with cold, mottled peripheries. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 78/48 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% on air. There are crackles to the mid-zones. There is no new murmur and heart sounds are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypotension?
questions.e: Extensive MI causing pump failure gives cardiogenic shock: hypotension, tachycardia, cold peripheries, confusion and pulmonary oedema without a mechanical cause.

steps.x: Large MI + low BP + **cold** + **wet** lungs, no murmur.

elim: Heart sounds would be muffled with a very raised JVP.
Pulmonary oedema means she is not fluid depleted.
Peripheries would usually be warm, and the cause is clearly cardiac.
Would give a new harsh murmur.

steps.x: **B. Cardiogenic shock.** Pump failure after large MI = cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has coronary angiography and PCI for an NSTEMI via the right radial artery. Two hours later he suddenly develops right arm and leg weakness and difficulty finding words. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular, and BP 144/86 mmHg. His glucose is 6.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?
questions.e: Catheter manipulation can dislodge atheroma or thrombus; embolic stroke is a recognised complication of coronary angiography.

clues: right arm and leg weakness and difficulty finding words
steps.x: Sudden focal deficit **hours after angiography**.

elim: His glucose is normal.
Would develop over days with fever.
Does not cause sudden hemiparesis with aphasia after a procedure.
Causes a cold painful hand, not hemiparesis and aphasia.

steps.x: **A. Embolic stroke from angiography.** Stroke is a recognised complication of coronary angiography itself.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has had stable angina for a year, always relieved by GTN within 5 minutes. This morning he developed central crushing chest pain at rest that has lasted 50 minutes despite three doses of GTN. He is sweating.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly suggests myocardial infarction rather than stable angina?
o: History of angina for a year
Pain over 20 minutes not relieved by GTN
Response of previous pain to GTN
questions.e: MI causes central crushing pain lasting over 20 minutes that is not relieved by rest or GTN, from prolonged ischaemia, usually thrombus on a ruptured plaque.

clues: at rest that has lasted 50 minutes despite three doses of GTN
steps.x: Duration **>20 minutes** and **no relief** with GTN.

elim: Both stable angina and MI cause central pain.
A risk factor, not a feature distinguishing MI.
A risk factor, not a distinguishing feature.
That supports his old diagnosis of stable angina.

steps.x: **D. Pain over 20 minutes not relieved by GTN.** Over 20 minutes, unrelieved by rest or GTN = think MI.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has 40 minutes of central chest pain. His ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF. A junior doctor wonders whether this could be pericarditis.
questions.q: Which ECG feature most strongly supports STEMI rather than pericarditis?
o: ST elevation in more than one lead
questions.e: STEMI gives territorial ST elevation (here inferior: II, III, aVF) with reciprocal depression (aVL, I); pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation without reciprocal change.

clues: ST elevation in II, III and aVF
steps.x: Territorial elevation with **reciprocal** change = infarction.

elim: Typical of pericarditis.
A feature of pericarditis.
Occurs in both.
Pericarditis also elevates many leads, even more widely.

steps.x: **C. Reciprocal ST depression in aVL.** Reciprocal depression favours STEMI over pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man walks into the Emergency Department with 30 minutes of central chest tightness and sweating. He is triaged. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Within what time of arrival should a 12-lead ECG be recorded?
questions.e: Every patient with suspected ACS needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of presentation to identify STEMI.

steps.x: Suspected ACS: the ECG decides STEMI pathway, so **immediately**.

elim: Far too late; STEMI decisions depend on the ECG.
This is the PCI window, not the ECG target.
Too slow.
Far too late.

steps.x: **B. 10 minutes.** ECG within 10 minutes of arrival.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has 2 hours of central chest pain at rest. Her ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6. The doctor wants the blood test that is most sensitive and specific for myocardial injury.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood test?
questions.e: Troponin is released from necrotic cardiac myocytes and is highly sensitive and specific for myocardial injury; it is measured serially.

clues: most sensitive and specific for myocardial injury
steps.x: Need a **cardiac-specific** marker.

elim: Also raised by skeletal muscle injury; less specific.
Tests for thrombosis such as PE, not myocardial injury.
Non-specific and slow to rise.
Rises early but is not cardiac-specific.

steps.x: **C. High-sensitivity troponin.** Troponin = most sensitive and specific marker of myocardial injury.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has 1 hour of central chest pain radiating to his back. His ECG shows ST depression in V5–V6 and troponin has been sent. He is about to be given aspirin, ticagrelor and fondaparinux. His BP is 148/82 mmHg in both arms.
questions.q: Which additional investigation is part of his initial work-up?
questions.e: Initial ACS work-up includes ECG, serial troponin, FBC, U&Es and a chest X-ray, which helps exclude alternatives such as dissection and shows pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: Routine first-line tests in suspected ACS: bloods and a **CXR**.

elim: Used in stable chest pain, not ACS.
Dangerous in a possible ACS.
Not an initial investigation in ACS.
Not a routine initial test.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** ACS work-up: ECG, serial troponin, FBC, U&Es, chest X-ray.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man attends his GP 4 days after an episode of severe central chest pain and sweating that lasted 2 hours at home. He is now pain free. His ECG shows Q waves in II, III and aVF.
questions.q: Which is the most likely result of a troponin test today?
o: Normal, as troponin clears within 24 hours
Normal, because he is pain free
Raised only if he has renal failure
Undetectable, as only creatine kinase rises
questions.e: Troponin rises within hours of infarction and stays raised for days, so it can confirm a recent MI in a late presenter; that is also why serial measurements are used.

clues: Q waves in II, III and aVF
steps.x: Late presentation; troponin **stays up for days**.

elim: Troponin stays raised for days.
Being pain free does not clear troponin.
The infarction itself explains a raised troponin.
Troponin is the marker of choice and is raised.

steps.x: **D. Still raised.** Troponin rises within hours and stays raised for days (up to ~2 weeks).

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman is 3 days after an inferior STEMI. She suddenly develops severe breathlessness and pink frothy sputum. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg and oxygen saturation 86% on air. There are crackles throughout both lungs and a new loud murmur at the apex.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Sudden pulmonary oedema with a new apical murmur after inferior MI suggests papillary muscle rupture (posteromedial, single coronary supply) with acute severe MR; echocardiography confirms it.

clues: new loud murmur at the apex
steps.x: Mechanical complication suspected: image the **valves**.

elim: PE is less likely with a new murmur after MI.
Dangerous and not diagnostic here.
Will be raised from the MI and will not show the mechanical cause.
Tests for PE, not a valve lesion.

steps.x: **D. Transthoracic echocardiogram.** Any new murmur after MI: urgent echo.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had 70 minutes of central crushing chest pain. His ECG shows ST elevation in V2–V5. The PCI team has been called. He has no allergies or bleeding history and has not taken anything yet. His oxygen saturation is 97% on air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate drug treatment?
questions.e: Aspirin 300 mg is given immediately in suspected MI, followed by a second antiplatelet (ticagrelor or clopidogrel or prasugrel) and anticoagulation.

steps.x: First drug in **any** ACS.

elim: Not part of immediate ACS treatment.
A loading dose of a second antiplatelet is given with aspirin, not alone at maintenance dose.
Not used in acute STEMI.
Not used in acute STEMI.

steps.x: **A. Aspirin 300 mg.** Give aspirin 300 mg immediately.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has 40 minutes of central chest pain with ST depression in V4–V6. She has been given aspirin. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 142/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. A student asks whether she needs oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate oxygen management?
o: High-flow oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask
questions.e: Oxygen is given in ACS only if hypoxic (saturations below 94%); pain is treated with GTN and IV morphine.

steps.x: Saturations are **97%**: no hypoxia.

elim: Not needed with saturations of 97%.
For pulmonary oedema with hypoxia, not here.
Hyperoxia may harm ischaemic myocardium; only give if sats are below 94%.
She is not hypoxic.

steps.x: **D. No supplemental oxygen.** ACS: oxygen only if sats <94%.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with an inferior NSTEMI has had aspirin, ticagrelor and fondaparinux. Despite two doses of sublingual GTN he is still in severe pain and distressed. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. He has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step for his pain?
questions.e: Pain in ACS is treated with GTN and, if it persists, IV morphine (with an antiemetic).

clues: Despite two doses of sublingual GTN
steps.x: GTN failed: **IV opioid**.

elim: NSAIDs are avoided in ACS (increase cardiovascular risk and bleeding with antiplatelets).
Too weak for ischaemic pain.
Too slow and weak for acute ischaemic pain.
Can cause sudden hypotension and reflex tachycardia.

steps.x: **B. IV morphine with an antiemetic.** ACS pain: GTN then IV morphine.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has an NSTEMI with ST depression in V3–V6 and a raised troponin. She has been given aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel. Her creatinine is 96 µmol/L and she has no bleeding risk factors. An anticoagulant is now needed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
questions.e: In NSTEMI, aspirin and a second antiplatelet are given with anticoagulation using fondaparinux (or heparin).

steps.x: NSTEMI anticoagulant with normal renal function.

elim: A thrombolytic, used only in STEMI when PCI is not available.
Not used for acute NSTEMI anticoagulation.
Not used in ACS.
Not used for acute ACS anticoagulation.

steps.x: **D. Fondaparinux.** NSTEMI: aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor + fondaparinux.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has 1 hour of chest pain and anterior ST elevation on the ambulance ECG. The nearest hospital, without a cath lab, is 20 minutes away. A primary PCI centre is 50 minutes away and can treat him within 90 minutes of diagnosis. He has no contraindications.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Admit to the nearest hospital for medical therapy
Admit to the nearest hospital for troponin first
Transfer directly to the PCI centre for primary PCI
questions.e: STEMI is treated by primary PCI if it can be done within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could have been given; bypassing a non-PCI hospital is right when this is achievable.

steps.x: STEMI and PCI is available **within 120 minutes**.

elim: STEMI needs reperfusion; PCI is achievable.
STEMI is diagnosed on ECG; waiting for troponin delays reperfusion.
Thrombolysis is for when PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes.
STEMI needs emergency reperfusion.

steps.x: **E. Transfer directly to the PCI centre for primary PCI.** STEMI: primary PCI if within 120 minutes.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman on a remote island had an inferior STEMI and received alteplase 45 minutes ago because PCI was not possible within 120 minutes. Her pain has eased and the ST elevation has fallen by 60%. She is stable.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue anticoagulation and transfer to a PCI centre
Give a second dose of alteplase
Refer for coronary artery bypass grafting
questions.e: After thrombolysis, anticoagulation is continued and the patient is transferred to a PCI centre for angiography.

steps.x: Lysis given and **worked**: what next?

elim: She needs angiography after thrombolysis.
Not indicated with successful reperfusion; repeat lysis is not routine.
Not the immediate step.
Anticoagulation should continue after lysis.

steps.x: **A. Continue anticoagulation and transfer to a PCI centre.** After thrombolysis: continue anticoagulation and transfer for PCI.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has an NSTEMI. He has been given aspirin, clopidogrel and fondaparinux and his pain has settled. The team now needs to estimate his 6 month mortality to decide whether he needs early angiography.
questions.q: Which score is most appropriate?
questions.e: After initial medical therapy, NSTEMI is risk-stratified with the GRACE score to decide between early PCI and conservative management.

steps.x: Risk stratification of **NSTEMI**.

elim: Stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.
Severity of pneumonia.
Bleeding risk on anticoagulation.
Probability of DVT or PE.

steps.x: **C. GRACE.** NSTEMI: medical therapy, then GRACE score.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with diabetes and CKD has an NSTEMI with dynamic ST depression and a high troponin. After aspirin, ticagrelor and fondaparinux she is pain free. Her GRACE score predicts a 6 month mortality of 9%, which is high risk.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Coronary angiography with a view to PCI within 72 hours
Discharge with outpatient CT coronary angiography
questions.e: High-risk NSTEMI (by GRACE) should have angiography and PCI if needed within 24 to 72 hours; low risk can be managed conservatively.

steps.x: NSTEMI, stable, **GRACE high**.

elim: High-risk NSTEMI needs inpatient invasive angiography.
Not for high-risk NSTEMI.
Thrombolysis is not used in NSTEMI.
Conservative treatment is for low-risk patients.

steps.x: **A. Coronary angiography with a view to PCI within 72 hours.** High-risk NSTEMI: angiography ± PCI within 72 hours.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has an NSTEMI with a small troponin rise and no ongoing pain. His ECG is normal apart from minor T-wave flattening. He has no heart failure, diabetes or kidney disease. His GRACE score predicts a 6 month mortality of 1.2%, which is low risk.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Low-risk NSTEMI by GRACE score is managed conservatively with medical therapy (further testing as needed), whereas high risk has PCI within 24 to 72 hours.

steps.x: Stable NSTEMI with **low GRACE**.

elim: No indication.
Not used in NSTEMI.
This is for STEMI.
Immediate invasive strategy is for unstable patients.

steps.x: **A. Conservative medical management.** Low-risk NSTEMI: conservative management.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is being discharged after an NSTEMI treated with PCI and a drug-eluting stent. She will take aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin 80 mg, bisoprolol and ramipril. She asks how long she must take ticagrelor.
questions.q: For how long should ticagrelor be continued?
questions.e: Secondary prevention after MI: lifelong aspirin, a second antiplatelet for 12 months, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg), a beta-blocker and an ACE inhibitor.

clues: aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin 80 mg, bisoprolol and ramipril
how long she must take ticagrelor
steps.x: Second antiplatelet after ACS: **12 months**.

elim: Too short; stent thrombosis and recurrent MI risk stays high.
Shorter courses are only for high bleeding risk.
Not the standard duration after ACS.
Aspirin, not ticagrelor, is lifelong.

steps.x: **B. 12 months.** DAPT for 12 months, aspirin lifelong.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is being discharged after a STEMI treated with primary PCI. His LDL cholesterol is 3.2 mmol/L and he takes no other medicines. He asks which statin he will take.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate statin regimen?
questions.e: After MI a high-intensity statin, atorvastatin 80 mg, is part of secondary prevention.

steps.x: Secondary prevention after MI: **high-intensity** statin.

elim: Primary prevention dose; after MI a high-intensity statin is needed.
Low intensity.
Low dose; not standard after MI.
Low intensity.

steps.x: **B. Atorvastatin 80 mg.** Post-MI: atorvastatin 80 mg.

questions.stem: A 54 year old car driver had an NSTEMI treated successfully with PCI 2 days ago. His echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 55% and no further procedures are planned. He has an ordinary car licence and asks when he can drive.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate driving advice?
questions.e: After successful angioplasty with LVEF of 40% or more and no further urgent intervention, car drivers stop for 1 week; otherwise at least 1 month.

steps.x: Successful PCI, **good LV**, nothing else planned.

elim: He must stop driving after an ACS.
Applies if not treated by angioplasty, or if LVEF <40% or further intervention planned.
Too long for successful PCI.
Too long for successful PCI.

steps.x: **C. Stop driving for 1 week.** Successful PCI: 1 week off driving; otherwise 1 month.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman had an NSTEMI and was managed medically without angiography. She is now pain free and ready for discharge. Her ejection fraction is 50%. She drives a car to visit her sister.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate driving advice?
questions.e: If the MI was not treated by angioplasty, car drivers stop driving for 1 month.

steps.x: **No angioplasty**.

elim: She must stop driving after an MI.
Only after successful angioplasty with good LV function.
Far too long for a car licence.
Too long.

steps.x: **B. Stop driving for 1 month.** MI without angioplasty: 1 month off driving.

questions.stem: A 52 year old smoker dies suddenly after 1 hour of central chest pain. Post-mortem shows a lipid-rich plaque in the proximal LAD with a torn fibrous cap and an overlying occlusive red thrombus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the coronary occlusion?
o: Gradual plaque growth to complete occlusion
Plaque rupture triggering platelet aggregation and thrombosis
questions.e: MI is usually caused by rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing thrombogenic material that triggers platelet aggregation and an occlusive thrombus.

steps.x: **Torn cap** + **thrombus** on top.

elim: There is a plaque with thrombus.
Embolism would not arise on a ruptured cap.
Stable growth causes angina; the cap is torn.
A wall tear with haematoma, not a ruptured cap.

steps.x: **D. Plaque rupture triggering platelet aggregation and thrombosis.** MI = thrombus over a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has an NSTEMI with ST depression in V4–V6 and a raised troponin. Angiography shows a severe, non-occlusive circumflex stenosis with TIMI 2 flow. A student asks why there is no ST elevation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his ECG?
o: Infarction of the right ventricle only
questions.e: Partial or transient occlusion causes subendocardial infarction with ST depression or T inversion (NSTEMI); complete occlusion causes transmural, full-thickness necrosis with ST elevation (STEMI).

steps.x: Partial occlusion = **subendocardial**.

elim: That would give ST elevation (STEMI).
Not the explanation with a culprit lesion.
Would show right-sided ST elevation.
Gives widespread ST elevation.

steps.x: **E. Subendocardial infarction from partial occlusion.** STEMI = transmural; NSTEMI = subendocardial.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman arrives 1 hour after sudden central chest pain. Her ECG shows ST depression in V5–V6. Her first high-sensitivity troponin is within the reference range. The doctor plans to repeat it.
questions.q: Which is the main reason the troponin is repeated?
o: The first sample was probably haemolysed
To check the response to aspirin
Troponin falls to normal within 1 hour
Troponin is not specific for the heart
Troponin may not have risen yet
questions.e: Troponin rises within hours of myocyte necrosis and stays raised for days, so an early sample can be normal; serial measurements catch the rise.

clues: 1 hour after sudden central chest pain
steps.x: Very **early** sample.

elim: No reason to assume this.
Troponin does not measure antiplatelet effect.
It stays raised for days.
It is highly cardiac-specific.

steps.x: **E. Troponin may not have risen yet.** Repeat troponin because it takes hours to rise.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man had an anterior STEMI 4 weeks ago. He now has central chest pain that is worse on lying flat and on deep breathing, with a temperature of 38.1°C. His ESR is 68 mm/h and a pericardial rub is heard. His troponin is unchanged from last week.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
o: Autoimmune reaction against exposed myocardial antigens
questions.e: Dressler's syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis around 4 weeks after MI, from an immune response to myocardial antigens exposed by necrosis: pleuritic pain, fever and raised ESR.

clues: worse on lying flat and on deep breathing
steps.x: Weeks after MI + **pericarditis** + fever + high ESR.

elim: No source; the timing after MI suggests an immune cause.
Would cause ischaemic pain with a new troponin rise.
Happens in the first days with tamponade.
Not linked to the timing after MI; troponin would rise.

steps.x: **A. Autoimmune reaction against exposed myocardial antigens.** Dressler's = autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI.
